title: Anomalous rotational-symmetry breaking in proton arrangement of surface-confined cyclic hydrogen bonds revealed by atomic force spectroscopy

paper_content.abstract: In hydrogen-bonded materials and biosystems, microscopic proton ordering, which is strongly influenced by the quantum nature of protons, underpins diverse macroscopic phenomena, including phase transitions, chemical reactions, biomolecular processes and collective proton transfer. Yet resolving proton arrangements and characterizing their quantum behavior at the atomic scale remain challenging due to the small size of protons and the lack of effective approaches. Here, we exploit bond-resolved atomic force microscopy and spectroscopy (BR-AFM/AFS) to probe signatures of proton ordering in surface-confined benzimidazole (BI) assemblies. By performing BR-AFS along the apparent H-bond between proton donor and acceptor nitrogen atoms, we extract information consistent with H-bonding directionality and signatures compatible with quantum proton delocalization. We observe anomalous rotational-symmetry breaking in the proton order of the cyclic hexamers, arising from the coexistence of both localized and quantum-delocalized protons. The chirality of a single hexamer can be reversibly switched by altering its adsorption registry combined with collective transfer of six protons. Path-integral molecular dynamics calculations unravel that nuclear quantum effects promote proton delocalization and concomitant reduction of donor-acceptor distance. Our findings enable atomic-level detection of complex proton orders, engineering proton-based quantum states, and elucidation of long-range proton transfer mechanisms in molecular architectures.
paper_content.introduction:
Hydrogen bonds are profoundly influenced by nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) owing to the low mass of the proton1–3. To fully understand many fundamental biological and chemical processes mediated by H-bonds–such as enzymatic reactions4–6, signaling7, and the dynamics of water8–the quantum nature of protons must be considered. In two- or three-dimensional molecular crystals, where intermolecular H-bonding motifs create specific proton arrangements9–12, NQEs can significantly impact proton ordering, thereby dramatically altering structural and physical properties. For example, quantum delocalization drives proton order-disorder transition and H-bond symmetrization in high-pressure phases of ice13, and promotes high-temperature superconductivity in sulphur hydrides14. Recent high-resolution scanning probe studies of small molecules on atomically flat surfaces in ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) have provided preliminary evidences for proton sharing, including water-hydroxyl complexes on Cu(110)15, long-range-ordered Zundel cations on Au(111) and Pt(111)16, and H-bonded one-dimensional 2,5-diamino-1,4-benzoquinonediimine chains on Au(111)17. However, these observations have so far relied primarily on imaging, while complementary spectroscopic evidence remains limited.

Another challenge is to extend the investigation of proton ordering and NQEs from small interfacial molecular systems, such as water18, to those with heavier skeletons10. In this regard, the imidazole ring represents an ideal candidate. Capable of both donating and accepting a proton, it serves as an important building block in biological systems, facilitating low-barrier H-bonds (LBHB)4,5. Moreover, single-component crystals of imidazole derivatives can achieve above-room-temperature ferroelectricity, with electric polarization switchable via cooperative proton transfer through the H-bonds (N−H···N⇄N···H−N)19.

In this work, we introduce an approach based on bond-resolved atomic force microscopy and spectroscopy (BR-AFM/AFS) for determining H-bond directionality in benzimidazole (BI) architectures on Ag(111). We reveal the conventional unidirectional H-bonding in linear BI chains, while in cyclic hexamers, we unravel ground-state proton orders featuring coexisting localized and quantum-delocalized protons (states 1 and 4 in Fig. 1). We further demonstrate that a single hexamer can interconvert reversibly among four proton-ordering states (Fig. 1). Changing the adsorption registry suppresses proton delocalization, whereas a collective six-proton transfer not only reverses the chirality of the cyclic H-bonds but also restores the non-classical H-bonds (Fig. 1). Our work highlights the important role of NQEs and the local environment on proton ordering, as well as correlated nature of many-body proton transfer20,21 within interfacial molecular architectures.
paper_content.results:
Probing H-bond directionality via force spectroscopy
The five-membered imidazole ring in the BI molecule contains two nitrogen atoms. For clarity, we refer to the pyridine-like nitrogen as “N site” and the pyrrole-like nitrogen as “NH site” (see Fig. 2a). Upon adsorption on Ag(111), the prochiral BI molecule transforms into a chiral entity, denoted as either the l- or r-enantiomer (Fig. 2a). At submonolayer coverage, BI molecules self-assemble into various structures, including extended molecular chains, closed loops and six-membered clusters (Fig. 2b), driven by attractive intermolecular N−H···N hydrogen bonding provided by the imidazole ring22. The chains grow along the 112 direction of Ag(111) (Fig. 2b), indicating a preferred epitaxy. To specify the N−H···N bond directionality in this system, it is essential to distinguish between the N and NH sites in the imidazole ring. Fig. 2c depicts a constant-current STM image of a single BI molecule recorded with a CO-functionalized tungsten tip (see also Supplementary Fig. 3), permitting submolecular resolution23. Note that a single-lobe feature appears on both sides of the molecule, adjacent to the N and the NH sites, with the latter being more prominent (cf. the molecular structure in Fig. 2c and the detailed discussion below). Using frequency shift (Δf) imaging in constant-height mode24, both pentagonal and hexagonal rings are clearly resolved (Fig. 2d), with slight expansion and distortion due to CO bending at the tip apex25,26. However, the N and NH sites cannot be differentiated.

To distinguish between pyridine and pyrrole-like nitrogen atoms, we performed site-specific force-distance spectroscopy [FS or F(z)], which records Δf changes as a function of tip-sample distance27–30. Fig. 2e depicts a set of F(z) spectra recorded along a path that traverses two corner sites of the imidazole ring (see dashed arrow in Fig. 2d). The left projection in Fig. 2e displays the Fmin values extracted from each F(z) spectrum as a function of the lateral tip position d along the path. The Fmin(d) curve exhibits an asymmetric M-shape, with two peaks of unequal height separated by ≈4.6 Å, matching the apparent distance between two nitrogen sites in the imidazole ring (cf. Fig. 2d). The right projection in Fig. 2e shows two F(z) curves extracted at the maxima of the two peaks in the Fmin(d) curve (cf. blue and red points in left projection in Fig. 2e), with Fmin(N) − Fmin(NH) ≈ 7 pN (cf. Supplementary Fig. 4). FS provides contrast consistent with differences between N and NH sites mainly through atomic-scale electrostatic interactions with the CO tip, reflecting the distinct electron density distributions of these two sites, as elaborated below. Notably, our results are consistent with prior FS characterization of naphthalocyanine molecule, which distinguishes the inner nitrogen sites with and without hydrogen31.

Next, we applied line-FS to determine the H-bonding directionality in an open chain (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. 5). Although the bright intermolecular contrast in BR-AFM image cannot be directly interpreted as an H-bond32–34, the probe-particle (pp) model reveals that the “bright line” arises from the relaxation of the probe particle (CO molecule) above the potential landscape formed by two neighboring atoms26. When the sharp line coincides with an H-bond, it traces the path between the proton donor and acceptor atoms. Accordingly, FS measurements were performed along the bright connections between neighboring imidazole rings (Fig. 2f, g), crossing two adjacent nitrogen atomic sites. Along the apparent H-bonds, characteristic M-shaped Fmin(d) curves are also obtained with the first peak consistently higher than the second (left projection in Fig. 2h; Supplementary Fig. 6d). Two F(z) curves recorded at two peak positions show a clear difference at Fmin (right projection in Fig. 2h), with Fmin(N) − Fmin(NH) ≈ 4 pN. Therefore, the H-bond directionality in the BI chain adopts a left-pointing N···H−N configuration (Fig. 2g and Supplementary Fig. 6). This assignment is corroborated by two additional observations: (i) the appearance of a dark depression at the right-side termination, attributed to a pyridine-like N atom35 (white arrow in Fig. 2f); (ii) the apparent length of the single (C−N) bond being greater than that of the double (C=N) bond (Supplementary Fig. 7)25. Although the experimentally measured apparent distance between intra- or intermolecular N and NH sites are systematically larger or smaller than the DFT-calculated values (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 6e) due to CO-tip bending, this does not hinder the accurate discrimination between the two sites.

Anomalous symmetry breaking in BI-hexamer proton order
Next, we focus on self-assembled BI hexamers, which are homochiral owing to their H-bonding motif. These hexamers adopt four different adsorption configurations (Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9), denoted as ∓8.5°-L/R or ∓40°-L/R. The rotation angle (∓8.5° or ∓40°) is defined between the high-symmetry axes of the hexamer and the close-packed directions of the Ag(111) surface (Fig. 3b; Supplementary Fig. 8), while the clockwise (+) or counterclockwise (–) turn is associated with handedness (R/L) of the cyclic H-bonds in the hexamer36,37. Fig. 3a, b show a BR-AFM image and the DFT-optimized adsorption geometry of the −8.5°-L hexamer. The center of the hexamer occupies an hcp hollow site (cf. Supplementary Fig. 10), giving rise to threefold rotational symmetry: the benzene ring in L1, L3 and L5 sits over a hollow site, whereas in L2, L4 and L6 it sits on a top site. Notably, the +8.5°-R also adopts an hcp-centered geometry with C3 symmetry (Supplementary Fig. 10b), and DFT calculations show that both enantiomorphic configurations are planar on the surface with nearly identical adsorption energies (Supplementary Fig. 11).

To determine the cyclic H-bonding directionality in the hexamer, we first analyzed bond-order contrast in experimentally obtained BR-AFM images but found no systematic trend (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). By contrast, applying the same analysis to AFM images simulated with different effective tip charge38 reveals a clear bond-order contrast consistent with the expected chiral motif (Supplementary Fig. 14), and we clarify this discrepancy below. To gain further insight, we performed line-FS characterizations (see also Supplementary Figs. 15–18). Fig. 3g depicts six datasets, measured consecutively for the six H-bonds in the −8.5°-L following a clockwise sequence (red arrow in Fig. 3a). Each panel displays a characteristic M-shaped Fmin(d) curve along with two F(z) spectra recorded at two peak positions (red and blue points and curves in Fig. 3g). An overall trend can be discerned: along the measurement path, the second peak in the M-shaped Fmin(d) curves is predominantly higher than the first. Therefore, the Fmin(d) curves show features compatible with a clockwise N−H···N bonding scheme in the −8.5°-L (Fig. 3b). For comparison, line-FS measurements were also conducted for the +8.5°-R hexamer, revealing a counterclockwise N−H···N bonding scheme (Supplementary Fig. 15d, h).

To further support our interpretation, we calculated electrostatic potential (ESP) of the −8.5°-L hexamer on Ag(111) using DFT and simulated both AFM images and site-dependent FS with the PPAFM code39 and a negatively charged CO tip40,41. The ESP map reveals that the N site has a more negative potential than the NH site (Fig. 3e). In particular, the simulated M-shaped Δfmin(d) curve with unequal peak heights for all six H-bonds (Fig. 3h, i), together with the corresponding Δf(z) curves at the N and NH sites (Fig. 3j), reproduces the experimental results (Fig. 3g), thus validating the line-FS approach for determining H-bond directionality.

A closer inspection of Fig. 3g shows that, for H-bonds L3-L4 and L4-L5 in the −8.5°-L hexamer, the two Fmin(d) peaks have nearly equal heights: |Fmin(N) − Fmin(NH)| ≲ 1 pN, (Supplementary Figs. 15i and 17c; Supplementary Note 2). For such H-bonds, the extracted F(z) curves at peak positions overlap near their minima (orange-highlighted plots in Fig. 3g). At a tip-sample distance corresponding to Fmin, the AFM image of −8.5˚-L shows a single-lobe feature corresponding to the N-site in the imidazole ring on the right-hand side of the BI molecule for H-bonds L1-L2, L5-L6 and L6-L1. By contrast, a double-lobe feature is clearly observed in L3-L4 and L4-L5 and faintly in L2-L3 (Fig. 3c). Similar patterns are also observed for the +8.5˚-R hexamer (Supplementary Fig. 15f). However, the equal-peak M-shaped Fmin(d) curves and the corresponding double-lobe AFM features deviate from the DFT-based PPAFM simulations (Fig. 3f, h). Such observations imply that the donor and acceptor nitrogen sites become indistinguishable, reminiscent of both symmetric H-bonds15,42 and LBHBs4,5, and suggest the possibility of proton delocalization within the H-bond. AFM imaging near Fmin, together with line-FS characterization on multiple as-grown ∓8.5°-L/R and ∓40°-L/R hexamers, consistently reveals anomalous rotational-symmetry breaking of proton order (Supplementary Figs. 19-21). This contrasts with the nearly C6-symmetric, flower-like pattern from the PPAFM simulation (Fig. 3f) and with the computed M-shaped Δfmin(d) profiles with unequal peak heights expected for equivalent H-bonds (Fig. 3h). Moreover, neither small biases (Supplementary Fig. 22) nor a CO-terminated tip41 perturb the broken-symmetry proton order, although it is not discernible by tunneling spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 23). In different hexamers, one, two or three of the six H-bonds exhibit signatures of proton delocalization. Across a total of 56 cases, the mean fraction of non-classical H-bonds is ≈40% (see Supplementary Note 3).

Unravelling proton delocalization via PIMD simulations
To examine the influence of NQEs on proton ordering in the BI hexamer, we performed ab initio molecular dynamics simulations using both conventional and path-integral schemes (AIMD/PIMD)43 at 50 K. Compared to AIMD, which considers nuclei as classical particles, PIMD treats both electrons and nuclei quantum mechanically, providing a more accurate description of proton behaviours17,44. To simplify the system, we modelled a gas-phase BI dimer (L3-L4) with its initial geometry extracted from the optimized −8.5°-L-hexamer/Ag(111) (Supplementary Fig. 24a; see also “Methods”). Fig. 4a depicts the probability distributions of a proton between two nitrogen atoms–N (donor) and N′ (acceptor)–as a function of reaction coordinates RC derived from PIMD and AIMD calculations. The RC is defined as RC = (RNH − RN′H) / (RNH + RN′H) (1) where RNH and RN′H are the instantaneous NH and N′H distances, respectively (see inset in Fig. 4a). The PIMD calculations reveal that the proton is delocalized between two nitrogen atoms, in stark contrast to the AIMD results, where the proton remains covalently bonded to the donor atom (Fig. 4a, b). Free energy is calculated from ΔF = −kBT ln P(RC) (2) where P(RC) is the probability distribution of RC and kB is the Boltzmann constant. Under full quantum description, the free energy profile features a double-well valley at RC ≈ −0.18 and 0.16, separated by a small free energy barrier of ≈ 6 meV at RC = 0 (Fig. 4b). This may considerably enhance proton tunneling, leading to the occurrence of proton delocalization (see a snapshot from the PIMD simulations in Fig. 4a). Conversely, the AIMD-calculated free-energy profile displays a single valley at RC ≈ −0.18, indicating that thermally activated proton transfer is rare. This is consistent with the relatively large classical reaction energy barrier (≈ 32 meV) computed for proton transfer in the H-bond of the BI dimer using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method with zero-point energy (ZPE) correction (Supplementary Fig. 24b).

We further analyzed the temporal variations of NN′ distance and RC (Fig. 4c) to reveal the connection between NN′-distance distribution and proton delocalization. At the quantum mechanical level with PIMD, the averaged NN′ distance decreases moderately from ≈ 2.7 to ≈ 2.6 Å, accompanied by the occurrence of proton delocalization, where the averaged RC approaches zero (orange-highlighted region in Fig. 4c). For AIMD calculations, the NN′ distance oscillates around an equilibrium value of ≈ 2.7 Å (upper plot in Supplementary Fig. 24c). Intriguingly, the time-dependent RC evolution obtained from quantum simulations reveals a change in the sign (lower plot in Fig. 4c), corresponding to a proton tunneling process from N to N′, which is absent in the AIMD calculations (lower plot in Supplementary Fig. 24c). Within the timescale (10−13 s) of the quantum simulation, proton tunneling from N to N′ only occurs once due to the low free energy barrier (≈ 6 meV), which corresponds to a transfer rate on the scale of 1012 s−1 based on the quantum transition state theory method applicable to water tetramer45. Accordingly, we infer a rapid back-and-forth dynamic behavior of delocalized protons, which underlies the nearly overlapped F(z) spectra recorded at two nitrogen sites of the non-classical H-bonds (orange-highlighted plots in Fig. 3g and Supplementary Fig. 15). Since line-FS integrates over time, it reflects the time-averaged proton positions.

Notably, in BR-AFM images non-classical H-bonds appear shorter than classical ones (Supplementary Fig. 25), consistent with PIMD findings (Fig. 4c) and prior theoretical predictions44. However, such geometrical effects cannot be reproduced at the DFT level (Supplementary Fig. 26). To capture the coexistence of localized and delocalized protons in cyclic H-bonds (Fig. 3c, g), we performed PIMD simulations of a constrained BI-hexamer/Ag(111) surface at 5 K using the reaction force field46 (Methods; Supplementary Fig. 27). Starting from the DFT-relaxed −8.5°-L hexamer (Fig. 3b), the N···N distances of L3–L4 and L4–L5 were shortened slightly relative to other N···N spacings (Fig. 4d; and Supplementary Fig. 27a). The resulting proton probability distributions and free-energy profiles for L3–L4 and L4–L5 are presented in Fig. 4e, f. First, proton delocalization occurs only in shortened H-bonds (≈ 2.4 Å)42, whereas for N···N ≳ 2.8 Å the proton remains localized at the donor atom (Fig. 4d). Second, L3–L4 and L4–L5 display unequal proton probability distributions and corresponding asymmetric free-energy profiles. In the gas-phase dimer (Fig. 4a), removing one proton yields two mirror-symmetric configurations that interconvert via proton tunneling, producing a symmetric probability distribution. In the hexamer, however, L5 retains a localized proton on its left side, whereas L3 is proton-deficient on its right side. Proton tunneling could therefore transiently generate a benzimidazolium cation at L5 and a radical BI species at L3. Although such fleeting states are not resolved in time-averaged FS measurements, they may account for the suppressed proton delocalization in L3–L4 and L4–L5.

Controllable transitions among four proton-ordering states
We demonstrate that a single BI hexamer can reversibly interconvert among four distinct proton-ordering states: two ground states containing non-classical H-bonds and two intermediate states in which classical H-bonds prevail (Figs. 1, 5). At liquid nitrogen temperature, STM scans induce conformational change of hexamers between two equivalent adsorption configurations (Supplementary Fig. 8, and Supplementary Movie 1). This implies that a single hexamer can switch between two enantiomorphic structures when the chirality of the cyclic H-bonds is reversed through collective transfer of all six protons (cf. Supplementary Fig. 11). To verify this assumption, we performed tip manipulations on hexamers at 5 K (Supplementary Figs. 28, 29; and Supplementary Movie 2). Fig. 5a presents an AFM image of a −8.5˚-L hexamer in its ground state (state 1; cf. Fig. 3c). After tip manipulation, the hexamer rotated 17° around its center (Fig. 5b). Line-FS analysis of this configuration (+8.5°-L) reveals that the clockwise H-bonding directionality persists, while non-classical H-bonds are significantly suppressed in this intermediate state 2, as evidenced by the downshift of the ΔFmin values for L3-L4 and L4-L5 relative to state 1 (shaded area in Fig. 5h). Intriguingly, +8.5°-L can be transformed into +8.5°-R (state 4) via multiple proton transfer induced by inelastic tunneling electrons47. The CO-tip was positioned above the NH site of a BI molecule (green dot in Fig. 5b), and the bias voltage was ramped from zero to 0.5 V while keeping the feedback-loop open. A sudden jump in the Δf(V) curves was observed at 0.36 V (Fig. 5g and Supplementary Fig. 30), matching the NH stretching mode energy (Supplementary Fig. 31). This operation re-established the non-classical H-bonds, yielding +8.5°-R ground state (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 32b, f). The reverse transition (state 4 to state 1) follows a similar pathway (Figs. 1, 5d–f; and Supplementary Figs. 33, 34), proceeding via intermediate state 3. Importantly, multiple-proton transfer could not be triggered in states 1 and 4, indicating that ground-state proton ordering of hexamer is interlocked with its adsorption configuration.

To rationalize why classical H-bonds dominate in states 2 and 3 (Fig. 5h, i), we performed additional DFT calculations (Supplementary Fig. 35). We found that, in states 2 and 3, three pyridine-like nitrogen atoms in the hexamer occupy top sites on Ag(111) (highlighted in yellow in Supplementary Figs. 32c, 33c), whereas in states 1 and 4, all pyridine-like nitrogen atoms reside at the hollow sites (Supplementary Fig. 11). This indicates a stronger interaction between the proton-acceptor nitrogen atom and the substrate in the intermediate state configuration, which is corroborated by electron-density-difference analysis, Δρ = ρAg+hexamer − ρAg − ρhexamer (3) where ρ represents electron density of each component. Δρ cross sections along the H-bond (∓8.5°-L) indicate greater electron-density redistribution beneath the top-site proton-acceptor nitrogen atom (N′) than that beneath its hollow-site counterpart (cf. dashed rectangles in Supplementary Fig. 35b, d). Strong electronic hybridization causes a pronounced tilting of the N′ atom’s σ orbital (lone pair) out of the in-plane geometry (a black arrow in Supplementary Fig. 35d), thus disfavoring proton tunneling.
paper_content.methods:
Sample preparation
Ag(111)/mica substrates were employed and the Ag(111) surface was prepared by repeated Ar+ ion sputtering at 0.9 keV and annealing at ≈ 700 K for several cycles. Benzimidazole (Sigma Aldrich, 98%) was fully degassed and then evaporated at around 320 K onto the substrate maintained at room temperature. At low coverage, the molecules favored the formation of hexamers, whereas high coverage led to the formation of extended chains and closed rings.

Synthesis of 1H-benzo[d]imidazole-1-d
The synthesis of 1H-benzo[d]imidazole-1-d (deuterated at the N1 position) involves exchanging the N–H proton with deuterium using a suitable deuterium source. To achieve selective N1-deuteration of unsubstituted benzimidazole, we employed an acid/base-controlled, divergent deuteration protocol specific to N-unsubstituted imidazoles, using trifluoroacetic acid-d (TFA-d) as the deuterium source (Supplementary Figs. 1, 2)51. This method enables selective labeling at the N1 position without affecting the aromatic rings or the C2 position. The reaction was carried out under acidic conditions with CF₃CO₂D (60 equivalents) at 130°C for 12 h. The extent of deuteration was confirmed by ¹H NMR spectroscopy, where the disappearance of the N–H proton signal indicated successful incorporation of deuterium (for details see Supplementary Note 1).

STM/AFM measurements
The scanning tunneling microscopy and atomic force microscopy (STM/AFM) measurements were conducted in a Polar STM/AFM system (Scienta Omicron) at 4.8 K with a base pressure of better than 2 × 10−10 mbar. The qPlus sensor used had a resonance frequency (f0) of 24.5 kHz, a spring constant (k0) of ≈ 1800 Nm−1, and a quality factor (Q) greater than 150000 at 4.8 K. A netched tungsten (W) tip was used in the experiment, which was pulsed and poked into the metal surface to ensure a clean, symmetric, and atomically sharp front edge. Oscillation amplitudes of 0.5 Å were employed. All STM and AFM images were recorded in constant-current and constant-height modes, respectively, using a CO-terminated tip unless otherwise stated. The bias voltage was applied to the sample with respect to the tip. AFM images were acquired at a bias voltage of 0 V. The scanning height (z) of AFM images is relative to STM setpoint on the bare Ag(111) surface, with z > 0 indicating an increase in the tip-sample distance, and z < 0 indicating a decrease in the tip-sample distance. Image processing was carried out by using Nanotec WSxM software52.

Statistics and reproducibility
All STM and AFM measurements were repeated on multiple samples and with different tips, yielding consistent results. The representative images shown in the main text were selected from reproducible datasets obtained under similar experimental conditions.

BR-AFS measurements
Force spectroscopies [FS or F(z)] were measured with Us = 0 V. To perform line-FS on an H-bond, a BR-AFM image was first obtained for the H-bond. Following this, FS measurements were conducted along the bright line between the two molecules. Finally, another bond-resolved AFM image was recorded after line-FS to ensure no noticeable drift had occurred. Short-range F(z) were obtained by subtracting long-range FS recorded on Ag(111) and converting Δf(z) to F(z) via the Sader-Jarvis method53.

Rotation and collective proton transfer via tip manipulation
Before manipulation, the tip was cleaned/sharpened by repeated pulsing/poking on Ag(111). For an as-grown hexamer (∓8.5°-L/R), the tip was placed over one molecule at Us = 10 mV, It = 10 pA; feedback was then disabled and the tip lowered until It ≈ 20 nA to enlarge tip-molecule interaction. Lateral motion at 1 nm s−1 rotated the hexamer into an intermediate state (±8.5°-L/R), which preserves cyclic H-bond chirality. We then imaged the hexamer, positioned the tip at an NH site, and ramped the bias until an abrupt Δf change at |Us| ≈ 0.35 V indicating collective proton transfer; a follow-up AFM image confirmed the ground state (±8.5°-R/L). The protocol was repeated > 30 times with high reproducibility.

DFT calculations and AIMD simulations
DFT calculations were performed using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP)54,55, with the projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials56,57. The exchange-correlation effect was described by the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof exchange-correlation functional58 within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA). The modelled adsorption structure consists of a BI hexamer adsorbed on the three-layer Ag(111) substrate of a 7√3 × 12 unit cell and the thickness of the vacuum slab is larger than 11 Å. During structural optimization, the substrate was fixed, and the cutoff energy of the plane wave basis set was set to 520 eV. Due to the large scale of the absorption model, the structural optimizations were considered converged when the maximum force on each atom was less than 0.01 eV Å−1. Only the Γ point in the Brillouin zone was sampled. DFT-D3 method with Becke-Johnson damping function59 was used to account for the van der Waals interaction for the surface adsorption.

In ab-initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) based on the classical nuclear approximation and the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) calculations, the cutoff energy was set to 600 eV and the degrees of freedom in z-direction were fixed. The maximum force on each atom was less than 0.005 eV Å−1 after the CI-NEB calculation had reached convergence. The AIMD simulations were performed for 1935 fs with a timestep of 0.1935 fs at a temperature of 50 K. The canonical (NVT) ensemble was sampled using the Langevin thermostat60,61.

Ab-initio PIMD calculation
Ab-initio based PIMD simulations employing 8 beads were performed using the i-PI software62, combined with the time-dependent ab initio package (TDAP)63–65 implemented in Quantum Espresso66,67. The SG15 Optimized Norm-Conserving Vanderbilt (ONCV) pseudopotentials68,69 was used to describe the core electrons. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional58 was adopted to describe the exchange-correlation effect. The kinetic energy cutoff for wavefunctions and for charge densities were set to 100 Ry and 400 Ry, respectively. The PIMD simulations were performed for 385 fs with a timestep of 0.1935 fs at 50 K. The canonical (NVT) ensemble was sampled with the Path Integral Langevin Equation (PILE) thermostat70. PIMD based on the force field was performed using the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS)71 and the reaction force field46.

The BI dimer was derived from the optimized −8.5°-L structure and pre-optimized in the gas phase prior to AIMD/PIMD simulations. In the calculations, one proton was removed from the BI dimer, resulting in a negatively charged species. This modification places the remaining proton in an asymmetric environment, which promotes quantum delocalization within the intermolecular hydrogen bond. At each timestep, the positions of the N, N′, and H atoms were extracted, the RC = (dNH − dN′H) / (dNH + dN′H) was determined, and all possible combinations were enumerated. The resulting probability distribution and free energy profiles of the reaction coordinate were smoothed using a 3-point discrete convolution kernel with a weight of [0.2, 0.6, 0.2] across 200 intervals, followed by a sliding rectangular window filter spanning 9 bins.

PIMD simulation based on force field
Force field-based PIMD simulations were performed using the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS)71,72 and the reaction force field46. The normal mode path-integral driver73 implemented within LAMMPS were used to carry out the simulations. A Nose-Hoover massive chain thermostat74 was used to sample the canonical (NVT) ensemble of 32 beads at a temperature of 5 K. The total duration of the simulations was 20 ps with a timestep of 0.2 fs. During the simulations, the molecular backbone (C and N atoms) and the substrate (Ag atoms) were fixed. The probability distribution and free energy profiles of the reaction coordinate were smoothed by applying a 3-point discrete convolution kernel with a weight of [0.1, 0.8, 0.1] across 200 intervals. The simulated BI-hexamer on Ag(111) surface exhibited an asymmetric structure (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 27), where the threefold rotational symmetry was broken by rotating molecules L2, L3, L5, and L6 by ≈ 4.8° towards L4 around the center of the hexamer.

AFM simulations
AFM images and force–distance spectra were simulated with the open-source probe-particle model26,39. Parameters: the effective lateral stiffness k = 0.50 Nm−1, radial stiffness = 30 Nm−1; oscillation amplitude A = 100 pm. The CO-functionalized tip was modeled as a dz2-like charge quadrupole41 with Q = −0.10 e (where e denotes the elementary charge). Tip–sample interactions combined Lennard–Jones potentials with DFT-based electrostatics computed for BI hexamer on Ag(111).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The paper investigates hydrogen bonds in cyclic hexamers of benzimidazole (BI) molecules on a Ag(111) surface using
STM and AFM with CO functionalized tips. Resolving the directionality and discerning classical hydrogen bonds (N−H···N)
from non-classical hydrogen bonds with quantum proton delocalization (N···H···N) is claimed. Manipulation between different
hydrogen bonding motifs by atom manipulation is investigated.
The quality of the data is very good. However, the interpretation of the results and the claimes made are not very convincing.
I do not think that there is enough experimental evidence for the distinction between classical and non-classical hydrogen
bonds. It would be great, but is not convincingly shown. Several questions remain open and need to be considered. I
recommend that the paper is reconsidered after mayor revision.
Overall, the data is of high quality. However, I find the assignment of classical hydrogen bonds (N−H···N) and non-classical
hydrogen bonds with quantum proton delocalization (N···H···N) not convincing. I also see a potential problem with hexamers,
that show both type of hydrogen bonds. If molecules have a classical hydrogen bond on one side, and thus either have a
hydrogen or no hydrogen bonded to that N atom, it requires the other N atom of that molecule to have no or a hydrogen,
respectively, and thus also a classical hydrogen bond, or they would become radicals, right? I can imagine a structure with
all non-classical hydrogen bonds. However, in the mixed hexamer, with both types of bonds, I see a conceptual problem.
This needs to be discussed in more detail, or maybe reconsidered.
1. I think it is also very instructive to consider the closed shell Kekule structure of benzimidazole. In it, the two bonds that
connect the carbon atom at the 5 membered ring to N and NH site are different. A formal double bond to the N and a formal
single bond to the NH group. The resulting bond-order related contrast with AFM is in line with the AFM image of the chain
shown in Fig. 2f. The formal double bonds appear shorter compared to the single bonds. Moreover, the related difference in
electron density above the two N atoms might contribute to the contrast mechanism on N and NH sites, as observed in the
monomer. The bond order of N-C bonds in the hexamers could be analysed.
2. In the hexamer the differences in bond-order contrast are less compared to the open chain. This should be discussed.
Might it imply that possibly in all hexamer structures all the H bonds are delocalized?
3. In a non-classical hydrogen bond with quantum proton delocalization (N···H···N), would it need to be symmetric? Could
not the proton be delocalized, but still be (in average) closer to one of the two N, allowing some asymmetry of the N···H···N
bond?
4. A structure that has in part classical hydrogen bonds (N−H···N) and in part non-classical hydrogen bonds with quantum
proton delocalization (N···H···N) as claimed in states 1 and 4 in Fig. 1 seems problematic to me. The molecules connecting
non-classical and classical H bonded segments have a “wrong” count in hydrogen atoms. That is having one classical
hydrogen bond in the ring should determine all other classical hydrogen bonds in the ring. It seems to me that non-classical
hydrogen bonds with quantum proton delocalization (N···H···N) should only be possible for either all bonds in the hexamer,
or none. Please discuss in detail how a molecule that on one side has a classical H bond, can have a delocalize one on its
other side.
5. Related to the previous point: In theory the hydrogen bonds with quantum proton delocalization (N···H···N) is only obtained
if one hydrogen is removed from one molecule (Fig. 4b). It seems this “trick” is needed because of the problem described in
the previous point. What is the charge state of the structure in Fig. 4b? Is it a neutral doublet, or charged?
6. Could a hydrogen possibly indeed be removed from a hexamer? Providing another possible explanation for the observed
switching and asymmetric contrast in the hexamers (and relate to the different 8.5 and 40 deg tilted structures).
7. The authors make not clear how they distinguish between classical hydrogen bonds (N−H···N) and non-classical
hydrogen bonds with quantum proton delocalization (N···H···N). More specific: How do the authors come to the specific value
of 1 pN, that they use to discern classical and non-classical N bonds? Why this specific value? Possibly, (N···H···N) bonds
might be asymmetric. Moreover, the molecules might be tilted slightly on the surface or their local adsorption environment
might be different possibly contributing to the Fmin difference, that is not related to the nature of the hydrogen bond. The
value of 1 pN to discern seems chosen arbitrary.
8. The authors state: “Notably, we found that the centre of the +8.5°-R also coincides with a hcp site (Fig. 3d and
Supplementary Fig. 7). This indicates that the mirror symmetry for freestanding 6-membered enantiomorphs does not hold
when considering their adsorption registries (Fig. 3c,d).” I do not understand the argument. If the center would not be the
same site, I would agree that the structures can not be mirror symmetric. I do not see why both structures being centred
around hcp sites makes the authors conclude they are not mirror symmetric. In fact they do look mirror symmetric to me. (Flip
at horizontal line in Fig. S7).
9. Related to the previous point: Is the energy difference calculated for the enantiomers in Fig. S8 significant? Or is it within
the noise (energy cutoff criterium) of the calculation?
10. The energies for adsorption under +/-8.5 deg (Fig. S8) could be compared with similar calculations for the local
adsorption minima expected at +/-40 deg.
11. The authors write: “Thus, our methodology demonstrates that H-bond directionality can be unambiguously determined
via line-FS measurements, offering a clear resolution to the longstanding debate over whether the bright intermolecular
contrast represents an H-bond or an artifact due to CO-tip flexibility [31,36].” First of all: what is the resolution to the debate?
(I fear the authors might mean that the contrast is due to the hydrogen bond). What is the reasoning? In this context, please
consider that you also state: “This feature was observed in the Fmin(d) curves measured for a single BI molecule and linear
chain (Fig. 2e,h), where Fmin(NH) is lower than Fmin(N).” Note, that you observed the feature also in a BI monomer, that is
in the absence of any hydrogen bonds.
12. Is the adsorption site of the structures shown and switched in Fig. 5 identical? That is, are the transition states 2 and 3
also centered around hcp sites?
13. Related to previous point: Can the 40 deg oriented structures also be switched or manipulated to become other
structures, e.g. the +/-8.5 deg structures?
14. If orbital resonances could be accessed by STM, might that provide additional experimental data on the type of hydrogen
bond?
15. Optional: The paper could very likely be greatly improved by performing experiments with deuterated molecules. Effects
of proton tunneling could be revealed very convincingly by the comparison of proton vs. deuteron tunneling. It could help
discerning conventional from delocalized hydrogen bonds. In the present manuscript the assignment and distinction of these
two bonds is not clear.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors present an experimental and theoretical investigation of quantum proton ordering in hydrogen bonds using
bond-resolved atomic force microscopy and spectroscopy (BR-AFM/AFS). They demonstrate that enantiomorphic
benzimidazole (BI) hexamers exhibit unique quantum proton ordering in their ground states, which can be manipulated via
scanning probe techniques. These experimental findings are supported by ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) and path-
integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) simulations, confirming the presence of nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) in the system.
This work is highly relevant to the study of quantum effects in hydrogen bonds and molecular self-assembly on surfaces. The
manuscript provides an important insight into quantum proton ordering and hydrogen bonding at the atomic scale. However,
to ensure the validity of the conclusions, the authors should address major concerns. Additionally, minor corrections and
refinements in figures and terminology are necessary.
Major Comments
1. The primary issue with the manuscript is the interpretation of hydrogen bond directionality based on force spectroscopy.
As the authors are likely aware, there is ongoing debate in the community regarding whether the contrast observed above
hydrogen bonds originates from the bonds themselves or other effects. Specifically, it remains unclear whether CO-tip AFM
truly images hydrogen bonds or if the observed contrast stems from other intermolecular interactions
(see, e.g., S. K. Hämäläinen et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 186102 (2014)). Since this assumption is fundamental to the manuscript's
conclusions, the lack of supporting data beyond point force spectroscopy is surprising. A straightforward way to validate
these findings would be to provide a series of BR-AFM images at different tip-sample distances to corroborate the
spectroscopy results. Additionally, the Probe Particle Model is a well-established method for simulating BR-AFM images
with high accuracy. Given that this code is open-source, the authors could perform their own simulations to support their
interpretations. Interestingly, my own simulations of BI in the gas phase did not reveal significant differences between the N
and N-H sites, suggesting that the observed contrast might be a topographical effect rather than a direct measure of
hydrogen bonding. Further scrutiny of the provided images suggests that the molecule may not be lying flat on the surface,
which could influence the total force measurements. Another noteworthy observation is the discrepancy in the minimum
force values extracted from Figures 2e and 2h, which range from ~10 pN to ~40 pN. The authors should clarify the physical
origin of this variation—could it be due to incomplete background signal removal? Additionally, why should the N-H site be
more attractive to the CO tip than the N site? This could be better understood by analyzing the electrostatic potential (ESP)
of the molecule or performing density functional theory (DFT) calculations of the force spectroscopy. The authors discuss the
role of adsorption registry in proton ordering, yet the specific electronic interactions between the substrate and the molecules
remain unclear. Does the Ag(111) surface actively stabilize particular proton configurations? Are charge transfer effects
involved in influencing hydrogen bonding? Additional discussion or computational analysis would strengthen these claims.
2. The manuscript suggests that proton transfer in BI hexamers is primarily induced by inelastic electron excitation from the
STM tip. However, alternative mechanisms, such as thermally activated or substrate-mediated processes, cannot be ruled
out. Have the authors conducted control experiments at varying temperatures or tip biases to exclude these possibilities?.
Can the authors also provide a mechanism explaining how inelastic electron tunneling induces
proton transfer?
3. Since all experiments are conducted at 5 K, it is unclear how temperature affects proton delocalization and tunneling.
Would quantum proton ordering persist at higher temperatures, or would classical hydrogen bonding become dominant?
A
discussion on this aspect is necessary.
Minor Comments
• Figures 3 and 4 require improved annotations to clearly indicate key measurements, particularly the extracted force-
distance parameters.
• The phrase “broken rotational symmetry” appears frequently but is not well defined. The authors should clarify its precise
meaning and implications.
• The introduction should provide a more detailed comparison with previous studies on quantum proton delocalization in
similar molecular systems.
• Typographical and Formatting Issues:
o Page 3, line 7: “proton delocalisation” → “proton delocalization” (for consistency with American English).
o Page 7, line 23: “image” → “images”; “Large” should be lowercase.
o Page 7, lines 24-25: The word “products” appears redundantly.
o Figure 3F appears misaligned compared to Figure 3B—this should be corrected.
o Figure 5: The red arrow is not explained in the caption.
o Supporting Information: Some materials (e.g., Scheme 1, Figures S1 and S2) are not referenced
in the main text. Their relevance should be clarified.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The study presents a compelling investigation into quantum proton ordering in hydrogen-bonded benzimidazole hexamers
using bond-resolved atomic force microscopy and atomic force spectroscopy. The combination of high-resolution
experimental techniques and path-integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) simulations provides strong evidence for proton
delocalization and nuclear quantum effects in a well-defined surface-confined system. A major strength lies in the ability to
manipulate and switch between quantum and classical proton-ordering states using an AFM tip, offering insights into proton
transport and potential applications in quantum materials. In my view, this research makes a significant contribution to the
understanding of molecular-scale quantum effects and merits publication, as it introduces both novel insights and technical
advancements in the field. However, I have several questions and comments that should be addressed before acceptance,
which I list below.
The study is restricted to benzimidazole hexamers on Ag(111), which may not fully represent biological or bulk hydrogen-
bonded systems. Surface interactions with Ag(111) may influence proton behavior in ways that do not generalize to solution-
based or gas-phase environments. I would appreciate a comment from authors whether the observed quantum proton
ordering extends beyond the Ag(111) surface? Would the same proton ordering be observed on weakly vs. strongly
interacting surfaces? Also, would this behavior persist in a freestanding benzimidazole hexamer or in bulk crystalline
environments? In any case, I believe a short justification on the choice of Ag(111) surface would be appreciated by the
reader.
The interaction of the CO-functionalized tip with the system could alter proton behavior, raising questions about the true
ground-state configuration in the absence of an external probe. Could authors comment on that?
How does the temperature as well as external electric field affect proton ordering? Could an external field stabilize or disrupt
the quantum proton sites? In case of temperature I would appreciate a comment why temperature of 50K was chosen for
simulations.
Have authors consider using other techniques to further confirm that the observation is truly quantum mechanical behavior?
For example, inelastic neutron scattering or high-resolution vibrational spectroscopy could confirm the quantum vs. classical
nature of the discussed proton behavior.
I also wonder whether an isotope effect would influence the findings? Would for example deuteration lead to observable
shifts in proton ordering, verifying the role of quantum effects? Could authors comment on that?
On a smaller note. Perhaps I am exaggerating, but in Fig. 4b and 4c, I notice that the PIMD simulation results appear to show
two maxima/minima on the acceptor side. I am curious whether this is simply an artifact of the simulation or if it could indicate
additional effects that have not been discussed in the main text. Could this possibly be related to proton delocalization
asymmetry or subtle interactions within the H-bond network? I also strongly suggest to mark in these figures as well as Fig.
4d which side corresponds to the donor and which to the acceptor, as this would help in correctly interpreting the data
without looking into them main text.
In Fig. 3e,f, I find it somewhat challenging to clearly distinguish the single and double lobes that the authors refer to in the
discussion. While Fig. 3i,j certainly help clarify the interpretation by quantifying the force differences, perhaps there is a more
effective way to visually enhance these features in the AFM images.
The following sentence is missing a verb: “It is important to note that although the experimentally determined apparent
distance between intra- or intermolecular N and NH sites systematically larger or smaller than the DFT-calculated values…”
Is there a reason the authors use "Supplementary Fig. 3" instead of a shorter format like "S3"?
In the Supplementary Information, the authors use hcp in italics, but in the main text, the formatting is inconsistent. It would
be best to standardize the notation throughout the paper.
It may just be my impression, but in Fig. 2e, it looks like the N site and NH site are not exactly chosen at the maxima, but
rather slightly next to them. Is this just an optical illusion, or could the authors clarify how these positions are precisely
defined? Additionally, I noticed a difference in the donor-acceptor distance when comparing Fig. 2e and Fig. S2c. in Fig. 2e,
the value is 460 pm, while in Fig. S2c, the value is 490 pm. Is this difference correct, and if so, what is the reason behind it?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The manuscript titled "Detection and control of quantum proton ordering in hydrogen bonds at the atomic scale" presents a
highly complete and data-solid study that utilizes bond-resolved atomic force microscopy and spectroscopy (BR-AFM/AFS)
to explore quantum proton ordering in hydrogen-bonded systems. In my opinion, the experimental data are of high quality,
and the observed phenomena are both novel and fascinating. The theoretical calculations, particularly the path-integral
molecular dynamics (PIMD) simulations, provide robust support for the experimental findings, offering a detailed mechanistic
understanding of proton delocalization and quantum effects in hydrogen bonds. Overall, this is an excellent piece of work,
and I agree with its publication in Nature Communications. However, several issues need to be addressed to optimize the
manuscript further:
1.Regarding the long-standing debate over the origin of the clear resolution in CO-tip-based chemical bond detection (i.e.,
whether the bright intermolecular contrast represents a hydrogen bond or an artifact caused by CO-tip flexibility), the
manuscript mentions that "line spectroscopy measurements can unambiguously determine hydrogen bond directionality,
providing a clear resolution to this debate." Could the author comment more on this conclusion? Why can local force
spectroscopy be more convincing in determining the position of the H atom than the features in constant height imaging like
Fig. 2f?
2.his work reports a remarkable observation of symmetry-broken quantum proton ordering in the ground states of chiral
cyclic H-bonds within BI hexamers on Ag(111), despite the symmetric adsorption registry as shown in Fig. 3c-d. To clarify
this intriguing result, could the authors comment more on this phenomenon? Could it be a local distortion of this hexamer
during the deposition of the molecules or a local imperfection of the Ag surface?
3.The PIMD simulations in Fig. 4 elegantly demonstrate proton delocalization in a gas-phase BI dimer (L3–L4). However,
the quantum behavior of the full BI hexamer adsorbed on Ag(111)—where six H-bonds interact cooperatively—might not be
fully captured by this simplified dimer model. Could the authors comment more on whether the dimer-based simulations are
accurate enough to describe the cooperative transfer of protons in a hexamer?
4.The experimental observations of symmetry-broken H-bonds and their manipulation (e.g., Fig. 3, 5) were conducted at 4.8
K, while the PIMD simulations (Fig. 4) were performed at 50 K. Why did the author choose this simulation temperature and
whether the choice of simulation temperature (50 K) impact the agreement between the predicted proton delocalization
behavior and the experimental results obtained at ultralow temperatures (4.8 K)?
5.The manuscript highlights the critical role of adsorption geometry in stabilizing non-classical H-bonds (e.g., symmetric H-
bonds in hexamers vs. classical H-bonds in chains; Supplementary Figs. 12–13). Could tailored modifications of adsorption
sites (e.g., substrate step edges, strain engineering) enable the emergence of symmetric H-bonds even in chain
configurations? And why is the delocalized proton only found in the hexamer?

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have substantially revised the manuscript, adding height-dependent AFM/FS data, isotope substitution,
extended simulations (DFT + PPAFM, PIMD, classical MD), and additional controls. These additions significantly improve
the robustness of the study.
The central claim—that AFM line frequency-shift profiles can reveal proton delocalization driven by nuclear quantum effects
—remains controversial, as electrostatics, adsorption registry, and fast hopping are not entirely excluded. Nevertheless, the
expanded dataset now provides a consistent and technically rigorous case that certain AFM signatures are consistent with
non-classical hydrogen bonds, and that these signatures cannot be captured by classical models or simple geometric
variations. With careful framing, this contribution will be of broad interdisciplinary interest and is suitable for publication in
Nature Communications.
I therefore recommend acceptance after minor revision, contingent on the following clarifications and additions:
General:
The manuscript establishes a correlation between AFM/FS signatures and the presence of non-classical H-bonds. However,
stating that AFM directly resolves or discerns proton delocalization seems too strong. I encourage the authors to moderate
the wording, using terms such as ‘consistent with’ or ‘compatible with’ rather than categorical claims.
Sections where the language should be softened
Abstract (p.2): “…BR-AFM/AFS to directly probe the proton ordering…”
Suggest: “…BR-AFM/AFS to probe signatures of proton ordering…”
Abstract (p.2): “…we determine H-bonding directionality and detect signature of quantum proton delocalization.”
Suggest: “…we extract information consistent with H-bonding directionality and signatures compatible with quantum proton
delocalization.”
Results, “Elucidating hydrogen bond directionality…” (p.4): “…FS distinguishes N from NH sites…”
Suggest: “…FS provides contrast consistent with differences between N and NH sites…”
Results, hexamer analysis (p.6):
“…Fmin(d) curves reveal a clockwise N−H···N bond directionality…”
Suggest: “…Fmin(d) curves show contrast compatible with a clockwise N−H···N bonding scheme…”
Summary (p.10):
“…a line-FS based method that resolves H-bonding directionality…”
Suggest: “…a line-FS based method that provides evidence consistent with H-bonding directionality…”
Some concersn that still need clarification from the authors:
Quantitative robustness of the classification criterion:
Report the number of spectra averaged per bond and provide error bars for |ΔF_min|.
Summarize the fraction of bonds classified as non-classical across all measured.
Height-dependent analysis:
Present Δf(z) traces at N vs NH with residuals from your fits, to show explicitly the z-range over which the classification is
stable. Indicate the uncertainty from the Sader–Jarvis conversion.
Internal charge effects:
Internal charge redistribution within a single BI molecule is expected to distort AFM contrast patterns directly impacting into
bond-length analysis from experimental images. Did the authors explicitly check for such distortions and compare with bond-
length analysis obtained from calculations? Please clarify.

Reply: The determination of hydrogen bond (H-bond) directionality relies on distinguishing
between the N and NH site in the imidazole ring. Our reasoning is as follows:
(1) We agree that the bright intermolecular contrast observed in CO-tip AFM images cannot be
directly ascribed to hydrogen bonds (H-bonds). We are aware that similar bright-line features
also appear in systems without H-bonds, such as silicon chains on Ag(110)1.
(2) Importantly, the probe-particle (pp) model reveals that the bright intermolecular contrast arises
from the relaxation of the probe particle (CO molecule) above the potential energy landscape
formed by two neighboring atoms2. When the sharp line’s position coincides with an H-bond,
it traces the path between the proton donor and acceptor atoms.
(3) Pyridine-like (N) and pyrrole-like (NH) nitrogen atoms can be distinguished using force
spectroscopy (FS or F(z)):
(i) For a BI monomer, FS were measured along a line intersecting two corner sites of the
imidazole ring. Plotting the minimum value from each FS along this path generates an
asymmetric F (d) curve with two peaks. These peaks correspond to nitrogen sites, with
min
the higher peak identifying the pyridine-like N site (Fig. 2d,e).

within an H-bond (Fig. 2f-h). This method enables determination of H-bonding
directionality in open chains (cf. Supplementary Fig. 6) and hexamer chirality (Fig. 3g).

scale electrostatic interactions between the CO tip and the two nitrogen species, which have
distinct electron density distributions.

follows:
(1) We performed LAMMPS-based PIMD (see methods) for the full system: a hexamer adsorbed
on the substrate. To reproduce the experimentally observed symmetry breaking in proton
ordering, we introduced a geometrical distortion resulting in varying H-bond lengths. During
the PIMD simulations, only the hydrogen atoms were permitted to move.
(i) Beginning with the DFT-optimized structure (Fig. 3b), which features threefold rotational
symmetry and nearly equal H-bond lengths, we induced asymmetry by rotating molecules
L2, L3, L5, and L6 toward L4 around the hexamer center at a fixed radius, sweeping an
angle of |4.8°| (Fig. 4d; Supplementary Fig. 27a). This adjustment reduced N···N
separations for L3-L4 and L4-L5 to ≈ 2.4 Å, maintained L2-L3 and L5-L6 near 2.8 Å,
and elongated L1-L2 and L6-L1 to ≈ 3.18 Å.
(ii) Proton delocalization in H-bonds strongly depends on bond length12, and occurs only in
the shortened H-bonds L3-L4 and L4-L5 (Fig. 4d). In contrast, for N···N ≳ 2.8 Å, the
proton remains localized at the donor atom (Supplementary Fig. 27b,c).
(iii) A key feature of the shortened H-bonds is the pronounced asymmetry in both the proton-
density distributions and the associated free-energy profiles (Fig. 4e,f). This indicates that
the proton primarily localizes near the donor site, with substantially lower probability at
the acceptor site of the neighboring molecule. This reaction is dominated by quantum
tunneling, thereby reducing the effective free-energy barrier to a few meV.
(iv) We further compare the proton delocalization in the gas-phase BI dimer with that in the
adsorbed hexamer. In the gas-phase dimer, removing one proton results in two mirror-
symmetric configurations that interconvert via proton tunneling, giving rise to a
symmetric probability distribution and a double-well potential (Fig. 4a,b).
In comparison, in the hexamer the molecule L5 retains a fully localized proton on its
left side, whereas L3 is proton-deficient on its right side. As a result, proton tunneling
8
across H-bonds L4-L5 and L3-L4 transiently generates a benzimidazolium cation (L5)
and a radical benzimidazole species (L3). This asymmetry leads to unequal proton density
distributions and asymmetric free energy profiles, thus affecting the degree of proton
delocalization (Fig. 4e,f).
(2) Imidazole is amphoteric and undergoes autoprotolysis to a much higher degree than water
leading to high proton conductivity13. Notably, imidazolium cation (i.e., the conjugated acid
of imidazole) has a pK of approximately 7.0 in aqueous solution14. This means that in neutral
a
water, roughly 50% of the imidazole molecules are protonated. Moreover, gas-phase
computational studies reveal a proton affinity of ~941 kJ/mol at N3, significantly higher than
at other positions (N1 or the ring carbons)15. Protonation at N3 is therefore both kinetically
accessible and thermodynamically favored due to resonance stabilization and aromaticity
preservation.
In summary, although surface-stabilized protonated or deprotonated BI species were not
directly observed in the intact hexamer, our LAMMPS-based PIMD simulations indicate that
transiently formed protonated (e.g., L4, L5) and deprotonated (L3) BI species coexist due to
quantum proton delocalization in shortened H-bonds, albeit with lower delocalization probabilities.
According to our DFT-based PIMD simulations, the quantum proton tunneling occurs on a
timescale below one picosecond (cf. Fig. 4c). Consequently, time-averaged FS measurements
cannot directly capture these transient benzimidazolium cation and deprotonated BI species in the
hexamers.
